# The Marginalia

The first correction appeared in October, tucked into the margins of a battered copy of *The Sea Around Us*. Rachel found it while checking the book back in—a small pencilled note beside a passage about tides: *"Local spring tides run higher than this. Check the harbor records."*

She almost erased it. That was policy, after all. Pencilled marks were to be removed, and repeat offenders were to be sent the standard letter about caring for library materials. But something about the handwriting stopped her—small, precise, slightly tilted, the script of someone who had learned to write carefully, perhaps in an era when that mattered. She fetched the harbor records from the reference shelf, and the stranger was right. Spring tides in Kestrel Bay ran eleven inches higher than the book's general figures.

She left the note in place. She told herself it was laziness.

The corrections kept coming. Always nonfiction, always older books, always pencil. A field guide to shorebirds came back with a note beside the illustration of a dunlin: *"Bills longer here. Our birds winter fatter."* A history of the coastal railway contained a correction about a date—the author had the line closing in 1962
